projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Thomas McLaughlin was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. All right, ready? Okay, let's start out and just state your name, and spell your name.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, my name is Tom McLaughlin. My name is spelled M-C-L-A-U-G-H-L-I-N.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay, where did you grow up?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I grew up in Boston, Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And tell me -- when I say you can expand on it -- were you brought up at the north end or you were--

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: No, I was -- lived in a community called South Boston referred to as Southey. It was a peninsula sticking into Boston Harbor. Boston Harbor has four or five peninsulas one of which is called Southey, so it had a lot of nautical influence there. There were docks for ships and also several yacht clubs, so you grew up with boats all around you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And who were your parents?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: My parents were -- my father was a police officer - he was a police detective, and my mother was a housewife. She was formally a secretary and worked for the A and P headquarters in Boston at one time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I had four sisters; I grew up with four sisters and one bathroom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And where did you fit in?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was the oldest, fortunately.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay, how did you get to Wilmington -- let's go -- explain to me -- okay, you were in Boston, then you left Boston, or you went to school, and then you ended up at the Dupont?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I went to MIT and graduated in 1951, and I got a job with the Dupont Company.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And that's how you got to --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I came to Wilmington. Being single, they started shipping me all over the country. They sent me to Louisville then to Charleston, West Virginia then to -- down to Louisiana then, finally, I spent a lot of time in Orange, Texas - the Gulf Coast.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay, where were you December 7th, 1941. What are -- were your recollections??

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was -- recollections -- I was out at a family outing. We used to take Sunday drives in my Uncle's 1938 Pontiac, and we were stopped at a Howard Johnson's near the Sagamore Bridge in Cape Cod, Massachusetts, and I was enjoying a triple malted milk with my sisters and some friends; and all of a sudden, he said, "The Japs have bombed Pearl Harbor." And I remember one of my sister's friends says, "Pearl Harbor is that a jewelry store?" And, then -- that was the only thing I remember about it was, "Is it a jewelry store?" So, that shows how very few people knew about Pearl Harbor unless you knew people in the Navy and heard the term used a lot; because, if you had friends in the Navy, they talked about Pearl Harbor. They talked about the Naval Base down in Rhode Island, Newport and things like that, and Great Lakes. So, I was familiar, and I knew what Pearl Harbor meant, so I realized then that we were going to be in war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And how old were you then?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was 16.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So, you were still in -- you were still in school?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was still in school, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: High school?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay, so, tell me -- say this again, in like, in December 7th, 19 -- say the whole sentence, December 7th, 1941, I was where?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was in a Howard --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No, no, say the -- repeat, "December 7th, 1941, I was --"

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: December 7th, 1941, I was out on a family outing. We used to take family drives in my Uncle's 1938 Pontiac, and I was with my sister and some of her friends and an aunt and uncle when we were out enjoying a triple malted milk when someone come in and says, "The Japs have bombed Pearl Harbor," and I remember one of my sisters friends says, "Pearl Harbor, is that a jewelry store?"

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, it was funny. I was telling you about Bill McLaughlin --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- and Bill McLaughlin was sitting in the stands and watching the Clippers play --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- and that was his thing, "Who's Pearl Harbor, and why are they doing those things to her?" So, okay, so, let's continue from Pearl Harbor. Where did you go from Pearl Harbor? Now, Pearl Harbor happened -- you were still a teenager in high school?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was a junior in high school, yeah. So, a lot of our friends -- you know, being a nautical area of Boston with a lot of peninsulas, everyone -- all my older friends were rushing to join up in the Marine Corp., so at that time, I had a discussion with my father who was a World War I veteran who said, he says, "Make sure you finish your education, get your high school diploma, and then you will be better prepared for what's ever going to happen." So, eventually I was -- at that time, I was a very avid model airplane builder, and I said which I should become a pilot, so I'll wait until I graduate and see if I can get in the Air Force. So, being -- I joined several model airplane clubs, and I was building planes and models and flying them in contests, and I -- then a friend of mine -- and I had a friend, and we both were contacted by the guy that says, "You make model airplanes?" And I says, "Oh, yes." "I got a job for you in the summer vacation," and I says, "Where?" "At MIT. They have a wind tunnel over there, and they're doing aeronautical research, and if you -- they're looking for guys to make model airplanes." So, I got my first job at MIT in the aeronautical laboratory, and I made -- we're working on the design of the Grumman Hellcat, and they wanted to see how strong the wings were before they would flutter. I was assigned to this group called the Flutter Research Group; and in any job, they like to play pranks on you, so one day they sent me down to the wind tunnel saying, "One of the electrical connections is loose. Would you go in and find out?" So, when you went into the wind tunnel, you took your shoes off, and you had your socks on. You were in pants and jeans, or something like that. So, I went fooling around looking for the connection. All of a sudden, I heard a click as the door was closed, and the next thing I knew they were turning up wind in the wind tunnel. So, they had these mounts there, which I grabbed a hold of like this, and they ran the wind up to 200 miles an hours with me in the wind tunnel; my socks came off, my pockets opened, and all my -- fortunately they had a big net down at the end of the tunnel to catch things; and they were all laughing. I could see them all outside the Plexiglas window all laughing, playing a joke on me. So, they turned down the wind tunnel, and what I discovered is I had dandruff before I went into the wind tunnel. When I got out of the wind tunnel, I had no more dandruff. It came out of my hair. So I realized [chuckle] -- that was very funny. So, the first job I had was doing research for aeronautical engineering. And the next thing you know, I went over and volunteered for the Army, and there were programs going on where you could get a year or two of college in the Army; so I signed up for an outfit called ASTP - Army Specialized Training Program - and the song in the Army ASTP program - (sings) "Oh, take down your service flag mother, your son's in the ASTP." So, they sent me to Camp Wood, Texas where I learned to become an antitank gun; then I went to Texas A and M University for a while; then all of a sudden, one day they came in and said, "The program is terminated. You're all going to be reassigned," but this was just before the D-day invasion; and what happened, they were trying to get, you know, fellows for the day and D-day invasion. And, so they sent me to Fort Sam; Houston, Texas, and that's where they gave me a very strong in-depth interview, and they said, "What language can you speak?" And I said, "Well, I can speak German fairly fluently because I operated a ham radio station. I listened to German programs during the war. I was listening to their reports from the Russian front with short wave, and I could speak German with a fairly good accent, and I knew the German terminology for German technical military items." So, they assigned me to military intelligence, and I was assigned to an MP outfit which were going to become combat MPs, and our job was - the D day invasion - was to get the prisoners off the beach and back to England as soon as possible. So, we went in late on D-day - went in on trucks - and we followed the supply trucks in carrying ammunitions and food, and we thought we were guarding ammunitions and the food; but, no, because when those trucks were empty, we would have Germans on them going back to the beach. So I was -- I think that after D-day I didn't get a good night sleep for about four days; I was completely exhausted; and, of course, there was artillery shelling. And the other problem was when -- walking around -- look out or land mines because I learned -- my one walk down the road -- I wouldn't walk on the road -- I'd look for trees, and I'd walk along the trees where the roots were coming out far, and I know the Germans couldn't bury a land mine with the roots coming out there, so I'd jump from tree to tree -- be very, very careful -- because some of the people I know have stepped on land mines and lost their legs. It's a very messy business so -- So, we would start collecting the prisoners, and I'd have to interview them, line them up, and find a -- first thing you did with a German prisoners is you'd separate the officers. You could tell them by their insignia. All the officers had similar gold braid insignias on their shoulders, and the non-com's had white piping around their shoulder epaulet with little pips on it -- and you're looking for the guy with white piping and two pips he was what the Germans called Oberfeldwebel or the top sergeant - like this guy, the marine sergeant you see on the History Channel - you use the tough guys, you know. So who is the Oberfeldwebel? So once you establish who is the Oberfeldwebel, you tell him what you'd want done, and he'd give the orders. So, we'd get them back to the beach; and finally, we'd have some LCs coming in and they'd unload, and then the engineers had bulldozers, and they would bulldoze sand into the tank of the LST for ballast; and as we got on, I noticed they had a lot of garbage cans stacked around. I was wondering what it was for. And, they also had big boxes of toilet paper. And, then we'd march the German prisoners on, pull up, and take off, and head back for England. And, now, I know why they had all the garage cans there because all the German prisoners of war were always up getting sick - seasick - and those were the puking pans and the crapping pans, and we -- and we get to [inaudible] the thing on them, and put them on trains, and after seven trips across the channel like this, my company was reassigned to take the Germans up to Glasgow, Scotland and, the USS West Point - which was a big two stacker travel ship built just before the war. And they renamed the West Point. It was originally the United States - it was the biggest transport ship we had. It was on this par with the Queen Elizabeth and Queen Mary. So, they said, "Well, the company -- the escort company that's suppose to be on this boat didn't get here in time, so your company is going to take them back to the States." So, we got all these German prisoners on this boat and took off from Gourock outside of Glasgow, Scotland and headed back alone out in the ocean. The reason we went out in the convoy was, we were faster than any -- we were doing about 20-28 knots or something like that, and no German submarine could catch up with us. So, we got up on the first day out at sea and took the German prisoners up on deck for -- for whatchamacallit -- fresh air and exercise; and at first, we took a whole pile of officers up, and one German officer comes up and he says, (speaking in German)"Keine eskorte, keine eskorte." - no convoy. And I say, (speaking in German) "Wir brachen keine Eskorte, die wir zu schnell. - we broke the convoy, we are too fast." He says, "But, there are U-boats out there. The Geneva Convention says -- " And I says, "No Geneva Convention, we are too fast for the U-boats, if you have any left." "Uh, we have a few U-boats -- uh, huh-huh." And I explain to him, you know, that most of the German submarines have been sunk. (Inaudible German speaking) So, that was a great blow to him, the fact that we were up there with no escort. This means that everything we are being told on the German radio was false. Then they began to realize, "No keine eskorte" - they were all talking among themselves. So, the funny thing is that this ship arrived in Boston - my hometown - and we're standing up on deck, and I'm with my captain, and he says, he says, "You're from Boston aren't you? "And I says, "Yeah." And I look over, and I could see my house in the distance on the peninsula, and I says, "That's my house over there." And he says, "Well," he says, "You're going to get a shore leave when we get here." So, we pulled in, and we got all the Germans off into a big marshalling yard down by the pier there where the trains came in. So, we get them all on the train, and then we went back to the ship, and the captain says, "All you fellows have a three-day pass." And most of the fellows from my outfit were from New York so they were all running down and grabbing cabs and hitching rides to go into the South Station to get a train to New York. I went down and hitchhiked a ride to go a mile down the road to my house. (Chuckles) So, I had a bag with dirty laundry in it, and I walked into the house and knocked on the door, and my mother opens the door and almost fainted [emotional hesitation] and, I says, "Can you do my dirty laundry?" [Emotional hesitation] and that was a real surprise. And, so I had a three-day pass in Boston, and I was the hero. You know, back from the war - what happened to you and everything. So, then I had to go back three days later. I went back on the ship, and we went back to England, this time with American troops on board, and I discovered that I knew four or five people from Boston who were on that ship. You just walked down the deck and seen somebody you knew; it's amazing. They say if you walk through O'Hara you'll meet somebody you know. Well, the same thing was on these troop ships. If you walked around, you'd seen somebody you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, what now -- this was right after D-day?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When you went back to England -- did you go back to England?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Back to England then we went back to -- back to France again; and by this time, they had cut off the entire Brest Peninsula, and you could hear the guns -- there were still shelling Brest; so we were backing up the 94th Infantry Division, and they had come up to Saint-Nazaire and Lorient, and they were expecting to take these forts because this is where the Germans had their submarine pens which were all underneath 12 feet of reinforced concrete. And the Air Force came in and bombed and bombed with B-25s and B-26s, and they came out with B-24s and dropped these thousand-pounders, and they just bounced off the concrete. So they had a problem there where the Germans were underground in the submarine pens, and they couldn't bomb them out, so what they did is -- because they needed -- Patton was driving them toward Paris, so they needed somebody to hold the Germans - the [inaudible] Germans - from coming out of Saint-Nazaire and Lorient. So, I was assigned to that division as an interpreter; so in the process of several months there -- they had fights out in the field, you know, infantry patrolled and things of that nature, and we were capturing Germans, and they were capturing Americans. So, one day we got a call from the International Red Cross. They said, "We're trying to arrange a prisoner exchange with the Germans, and we want you to take about 150 German prisoners, put them on two and a half ton trucks, and meet us down at a place called Etell - that's near Saint-Nazaire. So, we got all the Germans -- we went back to the camp and told all the Germans, "Who wants to be exchanged?" They all raised their hands. So, we brought all these -- I thinking about 165 Germans in four or five two and a half ton trucks and brought them down to Etell and lined them all up. Then, all of a sudden, a boat comes across the river and there's the German officer in it, and then some more boats come over and, anyway, this German -- this first German officer comes over is a medic, and he says -- he lines all the Germans up and gives them orders in German. He says, "Open your mouth." In the army [sic] mund is the German word for mouth; but in the army, they use the word [sic] mou because that's the word for the mouth of an animal, and that was a joke in the German army "open your [sic]mou." And, so anyway, this guy comes down he was -- and he was a doctor, and he inspects all the teeth among the prisoners, and he's going (indicating) "You can't go, back, back, back. We don't want you here, bad teeth." They didn't have a dentist, and they didn't want anyone with bad teeth; so they were rejecting all of these Germans because of their teeth. So, anyway, then the next thing you know, decided to bring the American prisoners over, and we didn't inspect them. We just took them back right away. And one of the guys in my outfit recognized his next-door neighbor as a prisoner being returned. It was so funny. And, of course, we were very much concerned that something would go wrong during this ceasefire, but the funny thing is the German that first came over saluted the American Colonel and shook hands with him, and they had the German photographers there taking movies and the U.S. Signal Corp there taking movies, and I suppose these archives -- somewhere in the archives up in Saint Louis -- these movies; it was very, very, funny. So, then we went back and, took -- released -- carried out people back in the trucks in which we had taken the Germans plus, the un-exchanged Germans were very, very, sad; and then our boys were telling us about how they were treated by the Germans, that they were treated very, very well. And, of course, one of the -- there was a -- one of the German officers was complaining about some of the tactics of the American Army were very brutal and inhuman because they had -- one of the American Howitzer had put a shell into the local whorehouse, or bordello, and killed some of the best girls in Saint-Nazaire, and this was immoral, unconscionable war [chuckles loudly].

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, that was -- how soon after that -- oh, you were there until the end of the war; correct?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, but see, by the end of the war I -- later on what happened was there was a big change -- there was a ship coming in carrying the U.S. 66th Infantry Division, and they were torpedoed by a German E-boat off Normandy - off near Cherbourg - and they lost all of their communications equipment, so they were not fit for combat. So, what they did is they took the 94th Division which were holding the Germans in Saint-Nazaire and Lorient and moved them up to Strasbourg under Patton. And the 66th Division which didn't have communication equipment came in and took their place. So, at that time, my company was assigned to the 94th, and we are moved up to Le Mans, France to build a big prisoner of war camp, which we did, and then later on, as more prisoners came in, we kept moving forward and building prisoner of war camps and containing the prisoners.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Until the end of the -- until June or July of --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, and then we were in Germany when the war ended, handling prisoners there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I would be interpreting and interrogating German prisoners, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So, tell me, from that moment on, how soon did the Nuremberg trials come up and all stuff?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: They came up after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: [Inaudible]?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: The Nuremberg trials started, I would say,at the very end of 1945.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So, you were -- you stayed in Germany? You never went back -- you never came back?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I stayed in Germany, yeah; and being fluent in German, I was assigned to the Nuremberg trials, and I was assigned to a Counter Intelligence Corp. or the CIC. And I was assigned to a group called the Personality Security Office. We were responsible for the security of all of the judges and prosecutors in both U.S., UK, France, and Russia. And I was assigned to an American judge - Judge Parker - as his personal body guard. So, I had to -- I had to live in the -- they had a chateau outside of Nuremberg and Judge Parker and the U.S. Judge Biddle, Francis [Drexel](should be Beverly) Biddle was also there. He was the head U.S. justice, and, uh, he told me why he was sent to Nuremberg. Judge Biddle, he says -- see, Harry Truman was now President of the United States, and Biddle was the Attorney General of the United States when they put Tom Prendergast in prison; and Tom Prendergast from Missouri was a friend of Harry Truman, so Harry Truman got even with Biddle by sticking him in Germany. (Loud laughter)

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So, tell us a little bit about the, uh -- tell us about the trials?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, the trials were very interesting because I used to go in -- I was a -- when we weren't -- when we weren't guarding the judges, we had assignments to do, and sometimes the judges would go back to have the [inaudible] of the State under guard of the 1st Infantry Division, and we sometimes would have to come into the courthouse and help sift through the documents - reading German, you know. And, one night I was in there, and they had Hermann Goering in there, and I served Hermann Goering a cup of coffee, and he thanked me for it. And, but it was sort of funny because we developed a rapport with most of the German Nazi leaders, you know. They knew that they weren't going to get away with anything, and a lot of them were very cooperative. Some of them were very stupid like Julius Streicher. He was a very ignorant, uncouth man. He couldn't even speak good German. And, the most intelligent, I think, was - this guy was head of their war industry - Albert Spear. He was very, very eloquent, speaks very good English. He was very, very intelligent, very cooperative. And, even Hermann Goering liked to tell jokes occasionally. But, we didn't get a chance to see these people unless there was special interrogations going on. But we came into the -- my commanding officer his name was Ralph Hortonberger (ph), and he was Jewish and had escaped Germany as a young man and he was -- I was assigned to the CIC. This was part of the CIC - Counter Intelligence Corp - and I walked into the courtroom one day with him, and we went to sit at -- we had what they call gray passes. We could sit at a prosecutor's table if no one was there. We walk in, we're standing there, and he's talking with somebody; and Goering takes a look at him - and he was one of the guys that captured Goering - and Goering just looks at him like this,(motions) and he nudges Hess, and I was standing right behind him, and I heard Goering say to Hess, (speaking in German) - "There's the son-of-a-bitch that captured me." (Laughter) and Hess looks over, looks back, looks over and (speaking in German) very funny.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What -- let me ask you -- we'll go -- okay, after the war, let's go after the war. Okay, so you got -- when did you finish your active duty, then where did you go? So tell me about from after the Nuremberg trials when you got out --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Okay, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: --you got out you went back to MIT?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, I didn't --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- whatever?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I didn't stay until the end of the trials because my -- I had what is points, everyone had points -- and my points came up, and I got transferred to an outfit doing MP duty in Frankfurt, and, then I got moved to a place in Lemoore (ph), Belgium. It was a holding camp and then they finally put us on a boat back to the states.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me the whole --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, all I know is we -- they kept telling us, well, you got a number of points and we'd -- you'd go by every morning for roster, and they'd call people up. Then, all of a sudden, your name would come up, and you'd go out on the truck that day to another camp. Then they took us to, Antwerp and put us on a boat. I think it was an old troop ship call the George Washington, and after a -- considering that we came back with the first German prisoners to Boston in three days on the West Point, it took us about three weeks on this tug. We had the bilges over flowing and everything. The food was lousy, oh, God. You see, now, the war is over. Now, they're giving you shit to eat. (Laughter). And, so, finally, it got into New York, and I was transferred up to Fort Devens and discharged honorably. And I was able to keep my German Luger pistol hidden all the time, and in the process, they said -- we were told on the boat -- this Major comes up and says, he says, "Okay, now, here are the rules: does anyone have a submachine gun in their loot? No submachine guns are permitted you know." Some guys had to give up their Schmeisser - their German pistols - machine pistols. And I had two guns. I had a German Luger and a Belgium Browning automatic, both 9mm pistols; so I gave up my Belgium Browning. Then, when I finally got to Camp Shanks in New York, they said, "Anybody that's got their loot this far, you have it." So, I could have come back with two pistols but I just came back with a German Luger.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Then what happened, you got out --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I got out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- then what did you do?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Then I got out and joined the 5220 club. That was a -- everybody that was a veteran got 20 dollars a week for 52 weeks. It was a famous, exclusive club. And, so everyone was a -- all my friends and I would all go into Park Square in Boston once a week and sign up that we're not working, and they'd give us 20 dollars. So, that's where we were having -- we'd go to baseball games and things like that all on the 20 dollars. Go down and have a cheap beer and was living it up. And then -- then I decided I had some friends back at MIT in the wind tunnel in the air nautical lab, so I went back there, and I got an application and filled it out, and then I went to a prep school for about six months to get my score up, and then I was accepted to MIT the class of 1951. This was in the fall of 1947; that's when I started. Then after MIT I studied chemical engineering and, I did a thesis at MIT. I had a translation of German wartime documents and, one was some documents from -- by a German inventor by the name of Kousch (ph) who was the great expert on hydrogen peroxide as a rocket fuel; and at that time, the U.S. Navy had captured some German miniature submarines which were propelled by hydrogen peroxide, and the Navy was interested in developing two-men submarines, and it was based on hydrogen peroxide powering. So, I was the first guy to ever measure the viscosity of 100 percent hydrogen peroxide vapors without blowing himself up. So, in the course of doing this work, I have all these German documents, and there -- there'd be coroners statements about, "What did Fritz talk about at supper last night?" because the next day Fritz's plant blew up, and Fritz was no longer able to make hydrogen peroxide for Hitler. So, I translate all of these documents, and it was a very interesting subject. So, finally we worked out a way to pacify hydrogen peroxide vapors by using a new material invented by DuPont called Teflon, and we sealed the joints in our capillary tubes with Teflon gaskets which the Germans didn't have at the time. So, we were able to operate with 100 percent hydrogen peroxide vapors and measure their viscosity through a capillary tube; but in the process of doing this, we had a couple of nice explosions, and I think it cost MIT something like 50,000 dollars for me to complete my thesis by repairing the laboratory. I used to look through a slit in an armored plate - this big armored cabinet at the end of the building - and I had to look through like a tank slit - like a tank driver uses - there's a slit in the periscope to read the instruments; and all of a sudden, everything was going blank, and you'd hear a big "Boom" and everything is blank.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did, D-day -- actually not D-day but -- V-day, you were in Germany then; right?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: No, I was in France. Oh, VE-day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: V-day?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: VE-day I was, --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did you feel, who were you with, were you partying, were you -- what were you doing?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, we went out and had a few beers, and then we kept saying, "Well, now we go to Japan." And my company was put on hold, and I said, "Well, I can speak German, I can stay here." And the guy says, "Well, you're in the army now. If you speak fluent German, they'll send you to the Japan. That's the army. It's perfectly logic if you're in the army." And, I says "Yes, that's logical. That's absolutely perfect logic. If you're a German interpreter, they'll send you to Japan." And it was true because I had a friend - the name was Kaufman (ph) - and he was a refugee from Germany, and he was with me in ASTP, down in Texas A and M. He could speak fluent German, had lived in Germany, and guess where they sent him, Japan. And we used to correspond about the logic in the U.S. Army. I'm the only guy that could speak German and went to Germany. That set a record for the U.S. Army Military Intelligence.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- during -- I guess it was D-day. Was D-day -- was, was, I mean, I guess -- was D-day era -- time frame, uh, was that when you were in, like, real combat? I mean, was that real combat--?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- was that like the highest part of your combat era --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, it got within -- you could see German tanks at a distance - the tiger tanks - but they're about a half a mile away. And, you could -- Germans were still sniping, and a lot of them were surrendering, and there was a terrible stench of powder and dead bodies. Some bodies had been around now for about two or three days and was really stinking up the place.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- what were your thoughts? I mean when you were going over there then. You knew you were going to be at war. You were going to be actually in the battle; right?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Were you thinking about something else at the time or --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- you were young?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was young; I was young.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I mean, did you really care? I mean, were you really afraid or you were just --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I figured it was just like a big game or something, and all I would have to do is duck. After all, John Wayne could do, so could I.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you have any funny stories about your buddies; I mean, like, you guys going out and drinking or anything that's really funny and sing some songs with them and you guys get into clubs and your from Boston, and you like to sing a lot of the old Irish songs and stuff, I bet?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, but, you see, I was the only Bostonian in my company, so I took a lot of the jokes. They'd say, "No baked beans today" you know and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where there any Italian buddies --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was it Irish -- Irish-Italian thing or --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh yeah, there were a lot of things like that, and I certainly -- we used to kid one of the Italians. We'd say, "Gee, I wish I had gone to Italy because I can speak Italian." And the guy says, "What accent do you speak?" And one Italian would say, "Are you a swamp dago or a mountain dago?" (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- I mean, did you have any really close relationships with any of your buddies there that you still stay with or had before you were --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, I stayed in contact with two or three, but they're all dead now. I went to some reunions in New York, and each year there were fewer people coming, so finally the guys that was running the reunions all died. And, occasionally I was working -- I was working for DuPont one time over at the inaudible building on special assignment, and I was sitting there, and this guy came in with a briefcase, and went in, and he was a salesman, and he looked familiar, and we went into this office. And I said, "I've seen that guy before." The next thing I know he's coming out of the office, and I look at him again, and he looks at me. He was the chauffeur at Nuremberg that used to drive the -- Judge Parker's Cadillac. He had a Packard Clipper - an army Packard Clipper which was the most modern car in Germany at that time. This was a 1942 Packard Clipper made just before Pearl Harbor, and I looked at the guy, and I said, "Hey," and he looked at me, and he lived up here in Media (ph). His name was Ronny Blake; or something like that. So, anyway, we used to get together occasionally. But the funny thing was that in Nuremberg - when the judges were in at night - he and I would be dating some WACs, and we'd bring them -- drive them down to the Grand Hotel in Nuremberg for drinking, and I was sitting in the front seat next to him, and we had two WACs in the backseat, and this was the most modern car there. It was a 1942 Packard Clipper, streamlined, and we're parked in front of the Grand Hotel; and all of a sudden, this Ford -- two-door Ford putters up with two stars on it - he's a Major General - and he gets out of his Ford and looks back at this car and sees two WACs in the backseat and me and the chauffeur in the front seat, and he comes up and bangs on the windshield and says, "Whose car is this?" And I said, "It belongs to the judge in the Nuremberg war trials." And he says, "How does he rate a car like this?" "Well, he's a judge, sir; (salutes) yes, sir." [Chuckles] Oh, was he pissed off. He was driving around in a two-door Ford.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- what do you want -- let me ask you this, this is a pretty good question. What do you want generations to come and know and remember about World War II?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, I'd say -- first thing I'd say is it was preventable. The trouble is the people who gave us the warnings were ignored, but I think the first warning came from Anthony Eden in 1936, when Hitler took over the Rhineland. He was the one that said we should get together and go in and take out Germany right now, and no one listened to him. There were prophets; there was another prophet by the name of Homer Lea. He was a -- he was a guy -- an American living in China, and he wrote two books, one called "The Valor of Ignorance" and the other called "The Day of the Saxon" and he talked about Japan's future expansions, and he said that Japan would be the first nonwhite, non WASP, non Anglo-Saxon power to cause trouble in the world; and they did. They took over most of part of Asia before we had to fight them. And he gave the warnings in his book back in the 1920s - that Japan would be a formidable power in the Pacific. And, of course, a lot of people saw Hitler was just a settler in Germany, but no one wanted to do anything about it; and now, we've got the Bush brothers -- or the Bush father and son -- who tried to do this -- like daddy Bush, went into Kuwait and what happened? They didn't do the job right. And, now, junior goes in to Iraq not doing the job right. To run a war you need Generals not MBAs from Harvard or Yale

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay, did you have any favorite song --?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- from the war, favorite song?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, Lili Marlene. I used to listen to German radios and that had a lot of very good songs, very good music they had. They had good music, good tanks, and good artillery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Sounded like that one place had some pretty good women, too?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, [chuckles].

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Sing me that -- the one that you were talking about -- in the, in the -- tell me a little bit about that -- the little song you were singing about the special --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, about the ASTP.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, tell me the joke about that?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: [Sings] "Oh," was a song that went, "Oh, take down your service flag mother, your son's in the ASTP." That's the Army Specialized Training Program - which means you're going to college you're not in the army - you're in the army, but you're going to college. I don't know all the lyrics, but it was very funny.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Anything else you want to tell me that you can think of?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, one time we used to take a judge -- Judge Parker was very religious, and he liked to go to church every Sunday. So, being his body guard, I had to go to church with him. So, he struck up a very good friendship with one of the English judges - Sir Norman Birkett; and in fact, on Sundays we'd go over to Sir Norman's house and Sir Norman had a little -- had a little house outside of Nuremberg - a commandeered Nazi home - and he was there with his wife and his staff. So, we'd go over there on Sundays and have tea. So, this Sunday we went to -- we took Sir Norman to the services at the Mergendorf (ph) Lutheran Cathedral in Nuremberg, and there was a lot of U.S. soldiers in there and also a lot of Germans, and they had a special service for the Americans. So, as a preponderance, almost everyone in there was an American in uniform, and -- except for Judge Parker and Judge Birkett there was also a Major General in there, in the U.S. Army; and something went wrong. The chaplain couldn't make it, so we're sitting there looking at one another and looking at their wristwatches; and all of a sudden, this German sexton comes in, and he says, "I have bad news. American chaplain is delayed. He can't make it today." So we were in a dilemma, and, of course, some of the Germans were starting to chuckle; you know - these inefficient Americans. So all of a sudden -- all of a sudden, a voice comes from the back, and this Corporal walks up the aisle and gets on the bull horn and says, "I'm Corporal so-and-so, and I'm not a minister, but my father is." So, he conducted whole services from the pulpit - a corporal in the U.S. army, [emotional hesitation] and this really impressed me,[emotional hesitation] whew, because afterwards Sir Norman Birkett said to us, he says, "You know" he says, "That could only happen -- [emotional hesitation].

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Would you like a little water?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, I could, yeah --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Let me get you some water.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, sometimes I get very emotional thinking about some of these things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Listen, that's all right. (Pausing for break)

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: But, I would say that incident there in the Mergendorf (ph) Lutheran Cathedral was -- that really affected me because I realized right away it made a very, very good impression on this English judge because -- and we showed the Germans that we could do something when something went wrong (pausing to drink).

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Are you done?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, cap it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: We'll have to get you some brandy a little later.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Umm, Louis the XIII, a 100 dollars a shot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay, so, let's see, I think we pretty much -- can you think of anything?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I like to watch some of these history programs on World War II, and my wife is always nagging me, "Oh, you shouldn't watch those" and I say, "Well, I'm in some of these movies." And she said, "Which one?" And I says -- I would say I was in a movie taken by the Germans at the prisoner exchange."

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember that one -- have you -- have you seen yourself actually?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: No, but I saw movies of that area of Etell, France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right where they bring them --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Where they're bringing the prisoners over. I was in the background that day, but on all -- we had three exchanges with the Germans. Oh, yeah, one very interesting thing. Oh, I told you about the artillery blowing up the bordello and killing the girls. The Germans were very incensed about that - that's inhuman warfare -- blowing up a house of ill repute.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did, uh -- we actually have some footage. Did you know there was a U-boat that was captured off of Delaware?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And we actually had -- we interviewed -- I didn't interview him, but Parks did. I was there with him one day taking some still photos of, actually, two guys that didn't really know each other?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: They were in the footage when they brought the prisoners on shore.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I saw pictures of that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, I think that was U-421 or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right. Let's see, how old were you when you went in?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I was 18.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Can you think of anything else?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: My biggest shock going in the army was -- I was the -- having been born and raised in Boston -- when someone said beans -- there was only one type of bean in the world, Boston baked beans. I had never heard of lima beans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I can remember getting the brown bread?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Brown bread.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And the beans.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: And the hot dog, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And that was Howard Johnson's -- who was from Mass; right?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, that's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Featured that in every one of their restaurants?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You could buy the brown bread and the --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, that's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- and the canned beans?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, B and W or B and M or something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Baked beans and the brown bread.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So, you're living here in Wilmington?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yea, I live by Creek (ph) now. I used to live with a group of fellows from DuPont over in (inaudible) park. We had a townhouse over there - the four of us; and one by one, we all got married.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you got married late in life?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Smart man.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you have any children?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: No. No, I had all the fun when I was young.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Our good friend Rich Gordon (ph), do you know Rich Gordon?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: No. No, I don't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He was over in [inaudible] still is there -- still lives there. He was DuPont; his brother was DuPont. Okay. I don't know whether you knew -- did you ever meet Jim Fossen (ph)?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Does that name ring a bell? That was DuPont - my dad was -- I told you -- was in Seaford, was just a lovely house.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: The nylon capitol of the world.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, hopefully, Russ Peterson (ph)-- Russ Peterson, you know, was in charge of that project or was part of that -- Russ Peterson was part of that project --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, I know him, yeah

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- and actually was going to go to -- they actually were responsible for saving hundreds and hundreds of lives. Apparently, from the, I guess, the shock cord when they made them nylon for the paratroopers versus the hard -- apparently saved a lot of lives -- hundreds of lives.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I see him often. He's very much a part of the waterfront here; Russ is.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, I saw him at the airport a few years ago, waiting for a shuttle, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you work in Wilmington, downtown?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I worked at Chestnut Run, and I worked at the experimental station. I was moved around in DuPont, and then I came back to Chestnut Run. I worked downtown; it was a horrible place to work. I could see this incompetence coming on. One by one the PhD's would retire, and they would be replaced my MBAs. And, at one time I was assigned to work for this very obnoxious person who told me, he says, "Now, Tom, I want you to be on the ball. You have to give me a good record because I" -- he says, "I plan on being Vice President of this company in ten years." And you work for a guy like that - whew - you wish he was dead. He never made Vice President. He quit and went to Japan someplace.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, I have two ex father-in-laws, and the one was part of the Legal Department at DuPont - Ed Connelly (ph) - who was there when Herb -- I guess Herb Shapiro was still there too.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And, then Jim Fossen. He was all around -- he was up at Niagara Falls --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, I use to know Ned Kimmel (ph).

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: His father was the fall guy --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: -- one of the fall guys for Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: They're still -- still to this day, trying to, --

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: Get him a -- yeah. Well, since 9/11 we know we have other incompetents that are -- of a lot more higher profile.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, absolutely.

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: But, the thing is this, I went to several meetings in DuPont. We had some of these MBAs coming up, and we had a guy that was in charge of one of the polyurethane program, and we had plants - the Conoco acquisition - we had a plant in Matagorda, Texas; we had a plant in Victoria, Texas, and a plant in Orange, Texas all making polyethylene, and we were in this meeting, and they had people from all the plants. And, this guy had just been -- he had been on the fast track, going up there -- and he had been in this job for, probably, four or five months. And sitting around the table, he's asking people where they're from, and this girl says, "I'm from Victoria," and he says, "What's at Victoria?" And she says, "J Unit, making polyethylene." And he says, "Oh, how about that." He didn't even know he had a plant in Victoria making polyethylene, and he was on the fast track. (Sighs, shaking head) Then I realized the ship was sinking fast. I referred to these people as having MBAs in basket weaving.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, when did you retire from DuPont?

sp.speaker: Thomas McLaughlin
sp.p: I retired in '89. One day I was sitting at the phone at Chestnut Run and this guy calls and, "I'm so-and-so; I'm with (inaudible)." And he says, "We understand you're very knowledgeable in polyethylene." And I says, "Yeah." "Would you like to come and work for us?" And I says, "Certainly." And he said, "We understand you're going to retire very soon." And I says, "Probably within a year." And I said, "Okay, I'll take your telephone number, and I'll keep you in mind." And about the next day my supervisor came in and he says, "Tom, we're making offers to everyone. You're suppose to retire next year; but if you retire this year, we'll give you a special award package." And I smiled. Oh, is this beautiful. Isn't this beautiful? So, I called back the guy where he is and I says, "I'm retiring next week." (Chuckles) And I went over to (inaudible and interviewed with them and got a job. I was with them for four years as a consultant. So, this came as a real, real -- talk about "Sa" luck. You know, this was it. So, I went over there, and I went over to Italy -- my wife and I went over on a trip to Italy to do some work over there, you know. It was very nice, and I discovered the different policy. You see, (inaudible) being an Italian company, and it had a lot of Germans and French and Europeans; and nobody had an MBA or PhDs, and they knew what they were doing. And I looked back at what DuPont was doing, and I said, "Oh, my God, what a difference."
